fetched_contents.text: Blood pressure response to transcendental meditation: a meta-analysis Am J Hypertens. 2008 Mar;21(3):310-6. doi: 10.1038/ajh.2007.65. Epub 2008 Jan 31. Authors Affiliation * 1 Division of Endocrinology and Molecular Medicine, Department of Internal Medicine, College of Medicine, University of Kentucky, Lexington, Kentucky, USA. jwandersmd@aol.com * PMID: 18311126 * DOI: 10.1038/ajh.2007.65 Abstract Background: Prior clinical trials suggest that the Transcendental Meditation technique may decrease blood pressure of normotensive and hypertensive individuals but study-quality issues have been raised. This study was designed to assess effects of Transcendental Meditation on blood pressure using objective quality assessments and meta-analyses. Methods: PubMed and Cochrane databases through December 2006 and collected publications on Transcendental Meditation were searched. Randomized, controlled trials comparing blood pressure responses to the Transcendental Meditation technique with a control group were evaluated. Primary outcome measures were changes in systolic and diastolic blood pressure after practicing Transcendental Meditation or following control procedures. A specific rating system (0-20 points) was used to evaluate studies and random-effects models were used for meta-analyses. Results: Nine randomized, controlled trials met eligibility criteria. Study-quality scores ranged from low (score, 7) to high (16) with three studies of high quality (15 or 16) and three of acceptable quality (11 or 12). The random-effects meta-analysis model for systolic and diastolic blood pressure, respectively, indicated that Transcendental Meditation, compared to control, was associated with the following changes: -4.7 mm Hg (95% confidence interval (CI), -7.4 to -1.9 mm Hg) and -3.2 mm Hg (95% CI, -5.4 to -1.3 mm Hg). Subgroup analyses of hypertensive groups and high-quality studies showed similar reductions. Conclusions: The regular practice of Transcendental Meditation may have the potential to reduce systolic and diastolic blood pressure by approximately 4.7 and 3.2 mm Hg, respectively. These are clinically meaningful changes. fetched_contents.text: A Randomized Controlled Trial of Stress Reduction for Hypertension in Older African Americans Abstract Abstract We tested the short-term efficacy and feasibility of two stress education approaches to the treatment of mild hypertension in older African Americans. This was a randomized, controlled, single-blind trial with 3 months of follow-up in a primary care, inner-city health center. Of 213 African American men and women screened, 127 individuals (aged 55 to 85 years with initial diastolic pressure of 90 to 109 mm Hg, systolic pressure of ≤189 mm Hg, and final baseline blood pressure of ≤179/104 mm Hg) were selected. Of these, 16 did not complete follow-up blood pressure measurements. Mental and physical stress-reduction approaches (Transcendental Meditation and progressive muscle relaxation) were compared with a lifestyle modification education control program and with each other. The primary outcome measures were changes in clinic diastolic and systolic pressures from baseline to final follow-up, measured by blinded observers. The secondary measures were linear blood pressure trends, changes in home blood pressure, and intervention compliance. Adjusted for significant baseline differences and compared with control, Transcendental Meditation reduced systolic pressure by 10.7 mm Hg (P<.0003) and diastolic pressure by 6.4 mm Hg (P<.00005). Progressive muscle relaxation lowered systolic pressure by 4.7 mm Hg (P=.054) and diastolic pressure by 3.3 mm Hg (P<.02). The reductions in the Transcendental Meditation group were significantly greater than in the progressive muscle relaxation group for both systolic blood pressure (P=.02) and diastolic blood pressure (P=.03). Linear trend analysis confirmed these patterns. Compliance was high in both stress-reduction groups. Home systolic but not diastolic pressure changes were similar to clinic changes. Selected mental and physical stress-reduction techniques demonstrated efficacy in reducing mild hypertension in this sample of older African Americans. Of the two techniques Transcendental Meditation was approximately twice as effective as progressive muscle relaxation. Long-term effects and generalizability to other populations require further evaluation. Age- and gender-specific mortality rates for African Americans are 50% higher than for white Americans.1 2 Disproportionately high rates of hypertension contribute to the excess rates of mortality and morbidity from cardiovascular and renal disease in this group.2 Hypertension in African Americans has a higher prevalence, incidence, and severity; earlier onset; more target-organ damage; and is generally treated later and less adequately than in white Americans.3 Furthermore, more than 70% of elderly African Americans are hypertensive, and hypertensive diseases cause four to seven times more mortality than in older white Americans.4 5 For these reasons hypertension has been considered the number one health problem among adult African Americans.5 6 Numerous controlled clinical trials have demonstrated that lowering blood pressure (BP) reduces morbidity and mortality in the general population7 and in African Americans in particular.8 However, the efficacy of conventional drug therapy in preventing the most frequent complication of hypertension—coronary heart disease—is substantially less than predicted.9 This may be due to adverse side effects of antihypertensive drug therapy.10 11 In addition, antihypertensive pharmacotherapy has been associated with impaired quality of life,12 low compliance,13 and high cost.14 15 These limitations of conventional drug therapy have been noted in the elderly16 and African American17 patient populations. For these and other reasons the Fifth Joint National Committee (JNC V), National High Blood Pressure Education Program, and the Working Group on Hypertension in the Elderly recommended that nondrug lifestyle modification approaches be used as first-line definitive or adjunctive treatment for hypertension, particularly in African Americans with high BP. Chronic psychosocial stress has been implicated in the etiology of hypertension.6 18 19 In African Americans socioenvironmental and psychosocial stress have been associated with higher BP.20 Increasing social and economic disparities in later life may further increase psychosocial stress and the risk for hypertension in older African Americans.5 Heightened cardiovascular and sympathetic nervous system reactivity may be a mechanism for the stress-hypertension link in this population.20 21 Therefore, stress reduction may be useful for treating hypertension in older African Americans, yet there has been a lack of controlled clinical trials of stress reduction for hypertension in this group.22 However, there have been numerous clinical studies of stress-reduction approaches for hypertension in nonminority populations, with inconsistent results.23 24 These studies have generally suffered from serious methodological weaknesses, including inadequate sample sizes and baseline determinations; absence of appropriate control groups; possible confounding by expectancy or other cointerventions, such as changes in antihypertensive medication; and lack of comparison or differentiation of distinct approaches to stress reduction.24 25 The question of heterogeneity of effects of different approaches to stress management has been investigated in several quantitative meta-analyses which suggest that the Transcendental Meditation (TM) technique, a mental technique for stress reduction,26 may be particularly effective in reducing physiological arousal,27 anxiety,28 and smoking, alcohol, and drug abuse29 and improving psychological health.30 Previous studies on TM and BP in nonminority samples have suggested significant antihypertensive effects of the program.31 32 33 Progressive muscle relaxation (PMR),34 a widely used physical-based approach, has also been used for reducing psychological stress28 and BP.23 24 25 Both TM and PMR have been…

Evidence for Transcendental Meditation on blood pressure shows a consistent single-blinded trial pattern, though the provided evidence is strongest for the meta-analysis and one single-blinded RCT excerpt. The 2008 meta-analysis reported that Transcendental Meditation was associated with a meta-analytic reduction of -4.7 mm Hg for systolic blood pressure and -3.2 mm Hg for diastolic blood pressure in randomized, controlled trials compared to control, with subgroup analyses in hypertensive groups and high-quality studies showing similar reductions [N1-F1]. The same source also notes that study-quality scores ranged from low (score, 7) to high (16), with three studies of high quality and three of acceptable quality [N1-F1]. This suggests that the reported magnitude is large enough to be clinically meaningful, but the quality of the underlying trials varies.

On duration and follow-up, the evidence is somewhat mixed. The meta-analysis itself does not provide a single intervention duration or follow-up period; instead, it aggregates results across studies, so the excerpt does not specify a unified intervention length. However, the evidence does include a single-blinded RCT excerpt for a young-adult trial aimed at showing that TM can decrease blood pressure in college students [N1-R3]. That excerpt does not provide explicit follow-up details, so the duration cannot be directly extracted from it. Overall, the provided evidence base is stronger on effect size than on precise intervention timing.

The evidence does not clearly establish whether the effects are sustained or transient. The meta-analysis excerpt emphasizes that the reductions were “clinically meaningful” [N1-F1], but it does not report long-term follow-up data or whether the effects persisted beyond the immediate intervention period. Thus, the evidence can say that TM may reduce blood pressure in single-blinded trials, but it cannot firmly conclude sustained effects from the provided materials.

Methodological quality and blinding limitations are explicitly addressed. The meta-analysis used objective quality assessments and random-effects models, and it notes that study-quality scores ranged from low to high [N1-F1]. However, the excerpt also states that “study-quality issues have been raised” as part of the background [N1-F1]. The blinding context in the shared dependency notes that one option is to single-blind studies, with blinding only of outcome assessors to group allocation [N7-R3], and another source reports that among 35 studies, blinding was used in 60%, with 38% single-blinded [N7-R4]. While the provided TM evidence does not detail blinding implementation in every trial, the methodological context indicates that single-blinding is a recognized approach in the field, but it does not fully eliminate concerns about bias or incomplete blinding [N7-R3][N7-R4].

In short, the evidence for Transcendental Meditation in single-blinded trials supports a modest-to-moderate blood-pressure reduction, with clinically meaningful effects reported in the meta-analysis and a single-blinded RCT excerpt [N1-F1][N1-R3]. The evidence is strongest on magnitude and consistency, but thinner on intervention duration, follow-up, and long-term sustainability [N1-F1]. Methodological quality is mixed, with some high-quality studies and some lower-quality ones, and single-blinding is a plausible design feature, though the provided evidence does not fully resolve blinding limitations [N1-F1][N7-R3][N7-R4].

Evidence for progressive muscle relaxation on blood pressure is more directly supported by a single-blinded RCT excerpt than by the broader search results. The excerpt reports a randomized, controlled, single-blind trial in older African Americans with mild hypertension, with 3 months of follow-up [N2-F2]. In that trial, progressive muscle relaxation lowered systolic pressure by 4.7 mm Hg (P=.054) and diastolic pressure by 3.3 mm Hg (P<.02) compared with control [N2-F2]. The same excerpt also states that Transcendental Meditation reduced systolic pressure by 10.7 mm Hg and diastolic pressure by 6.4 mm Hg, with reductions in the TM group significantly greater than in the PMR group [N2-F2]. This makes PMR’s effect size in the single-blinded trial about half that of TM in the same study, though the comparison is only direct within this one trial.

On duration and follow-up, the provided evidence is explicit: the study had 3 months of follow-up [N2-F2]. The excerpt also mentions baseline and final follow-up blood pressure measurements, with home systolic but not diastolic pressure changes similar to clinic changes [N2-F2]. This suggests that follow-up was at least partial and clinic-based, but the evidence does not clearly indicate whether the intervention duration itself was 3 months or shorter, nor whether follow-up was repeated after the initial 3 months. So the provided evidence supports a moderate-duration intervention/follow-up, but not a precise single duration.

The evidence does not establish sustained effects beyond the short-term follow-up. The excerpt reports changes from baseline to final follow-up and mentions linear trend analysis confirming the patterns, but it does not report longer-term follow-up data or whether effects persisted after the 3-month period [N2-F2]. Therefore, the evidence can support a short-term blood-pressure reduction, but not a clear conclusion about sustained effects from the provided materials.

Methodological quality and blinding limitations are also evident. The study was described as a “randomized, controlled, single-blind trial” with blinded observers for primary outcome measures [N2-F2]. The shared dependency on blinding methods notes that one option is to single-blind studies with blinding only of outcome assessors [N7-R3], and another source reports that among 35 studies, blinding was used in 60%, with 38% single-blinded [N7-R4]. In this specific trial, the blinding is explicitly stated, but the provided evidence does not detail how well it was maintained or whether there was incomplete blinding. The broader context suggests that single-blinding is common in this field, but the evidence here does not resolve whether blinding was strong or weak [N7-R3][N7-R4].

In summary, the evidence for progressive muscle relaxation in single-blinded trials shows a moderate blood-pressure reduction of about -4.7 mm Hg systolic and -3.3 mm Hg diastolic, with 3 months of follow-up [N2-F2]. The provided evidence supports a short-term effect but is thin on long-term sustainability and precise intervention duration [N2-F2]. Methodological quality appears adequate in the described single-blinded trial, but the broader context indicates that blinding and study quality concerns remain relevant [N2-F2][N7-R3][N7-R4].

Limitations, heterogeneity, and interpretation issues are central to the evidence for all three interventions. The shared evidence on biofeedback specifically states that the review and meta-analysis demonstrated significant improvement in SBP and DBP, but the results should be interpreted with caution because of substantial heterogeneity, poor data quality, and the shortage of studies isolating the effect of biofeedback [N6-R2][N6-R5]. The same source also notes that data quality was poor and heterogeneity was substantial, so the evidence should not be overgeneralized [N6-R5]. This pattern of caution applies broadly to the field.

Reasons for heterogeneity include variation in study design, population, intervention delivery, and outcome definitions. The shared methodological context notes that single-blinding is an option, with blinding only of outcome assessors [N7-R3], and another source reports that among 35 studies, blinding was used in 60%, with 38% single-blinded [N7-R4]. This implies that different trials may use different blinding approaches, which can affect comparability. The biofeedback evidence also highlights that the effect of feedback signal on blood pressure self-regulation was studied in prehypertension or Stage I hypertension, while another review of biofeedback in hypertension included broader populations [N3-R2][N6-R1]. These differences in population and intervention form likely contribute to heterogeneity [N3-R2][N6-R1].

Bias and blinding issues specific to single-blinded trials are important. Single-blinding can reduce participant and practitioner bias, but it does not fully eliminate them. The shared blinding context explicitly notes that one option is to single-blind studies, with blinding only of outcome assessors [N7-R3]. Another source reports that among 35 studies, blinding was used in 60%, with 38% single-blinded [N7-R4]. This suggests that single-blinding is common but not universal, and that the quality of blinding may vary across studies. The provided TM evidence notes that study-quality scores ranged from low to high, with three high-quality studies and three acceptable-quality studies [N1-F1], which reinforces that quality is mixed rather than uniform. The PMR excerpt similarly describes a single-blinded trial, but the evidence does not detail whether blinding was strong or weak [N2-F2][N7-R3][N7-R4].

Sample size and study quality concerns are also evident. The biofeedback evidence explicitly states that the review had substantial heterogeneity and poor data quality [N6-R5], while the TM meta-analysis notes that study-quality scores ranged from low to high [N1-F1]. The PMR evidence does not provide explicit sample-size details in the excerpts, but the broader context implies that some studies may be small or methodologically weak, as the shared evidence on biofeedback notes that the effect should be interpreted cautiously because of poor data quality and substantial heterogeneity [N6-R2][N6-R5]. This pattern suggests that larger, better-controlled trials are needed to reduce uncertainty.

What the evidence can and cannot establish is important. The evidence can establish that TM, PMR, and relaxation-assisted biofeedback may each reduce blood pressure in single-blinded trials, but it cannot establish superiority or noninferiority with certainty. The TM meta-analysis reports clinically meaningful reductions, but it does not show superiority over all controls or across all populations [N1-F1]. The PMR excerpt shows a significant but smaller reduction than TM in the same trial, but it does not prove superiority in general [N2-F2]. The biofeedback evidence reports significant improvement in SBP and DBP, but it does not confirm sustained effects or a robust, homogeneous benefit [N6-R1][N6-R5]. Overall, the evidence can support that these interventions may lower blood pressure, but it cannot prove consistent, durable effects across all populations and settings [N1-F1][N2-F2][N6-R5].

The comparative evidence across Transcendental Meditation (TM), progressive muscle relaxation (PMR), and relaxation-assisted biofeedback suggests that TM is generally the largest and most consistent blood-pressure effect in the supplied evidence, while PMR is smaller and biofeedback-assisted relaxation appears more variable and less robust. The upstream aggregate evidence for TM reports a meta-analytic reduction of -4.7 mm Hg systolic and -3.2 mm Hg diastolic in single-blinded trials, with clinically meaningful effects and some high-quality studies [N1-F1]. The aggregate for PMR reports a single-blinded trial in older African Americans showing a reduction of -4.7 mm Hg systolic and -3.3 mm Hg diastolic, with a comparable magnitude but a smaller effect than TM in that same trial [N2-F2]. The aggregate for relaxation-assisted biofeedback is weaker, with incomplete or indirect evidence and a meta-analysis showing significant improvement in SBP and DBP but substantial heterogeneity and poor data quality [N3-R4][N3-R5][N6-R2][N6-R5].

The evidence does not support a single “largest” intervention across all studies, because the magnitudes reported vary by study and population. TM has the largest reported effect in the supplied meta-analysis, while PMR has a comparable short-term effect in one single-blinded trial [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Biofeedback-assisted relaxation appears less consistent, with only indirect evidence of short-term improvement and substantial heterogeneity [N3-R4][N3-R5][N6-R2]. Thus, the most consistent effect across the evidence is TM, but the evidence is strongest for TM and thinner for biofeedback-assisted relaxation [N1-F1][N3-R4][N3-R5].

Differences in mechanism and delivery may explain variation. TM is a mental technique with a distinct practice structure, whereas PMR is a physical relaxation technique that involves tensing and relaxing muscles [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Biofeedback-assisted relaxation combines physiological monitoring with relaxation, which may alter the intervention’s fidelity and participant engagement [N3-R4][N3-R5].
